title: 菩萨蛮·书江西造口壁
titlePy: Pú Sà Mán · Shū Jiāngxī Zàokǒu Bì
titleEn: To the Tune “Pusaman”: Written on a Wall at Zaokou, Jiangxi
author: 辛弃疾
intro: Standing by a river in the south, a general who longs to win back the lost north looks toward the old capital — and sees only mountains in the way. A short lyric where rivers, hills and a bird’s cry carry a whole country’s grief.
analysis: 这首词是辛弃疾路过江西造口时题在墙上的。上阕从眼前的江水写起：郁孤台下的清江水里，流着多少逃难行人的眼泪——这里暗指几十年前金兵南下、百姓流离的往事。作者向西北望去，想看见象征故都的“长安”，可惜被无数座山挡住了。“山”在这里是一种比喻：挡住视线的山，也像挡住收复北方之路的种种阻力。下阕笔锋一转：青山再多也遮不住江水，江水终究向东流去——这是全词最有力量的两句，表达了一种不可阻挡的信念。可是最后又回到愁绪：傍晚江边，作者正发愁，深山里传来鹧鸪的叫声。古人说鹧鸪的叫声像“行不得也哥哥”（走不了啊），这声音正好说中了他壮志难成的苦闷。全词借景抒情（借写景物来表达感情），句句写山水，句句是心事。
analysisEn: Xin Qiji wrote this lyric on a wall at Zaokou, a river stop in Jiangxi. The first half starts with what he sees: the clear river below Yugu Terrace. But he asks how many refugees’ tears are in that water — a quiet reminder of the years when Jurchen armies swept south and ordinary people fled for their lives. He looks northwest toward “Chang’an”, the old capital that stands for the lost north, and sees only mountains, one after another. The mountains block his view, and they also stand for everything that blocks the road back north. Then the second half turns: however many green hills there are, they cannot stop the river — in the end it flows east. These two lines are the strongest in the poem, a stubborn belief that what is right will get through. Yet the lyric closes in sorrow again. At dusk by the river he is full of worry, and from deep in the hills comes the call of the partridge. People said the bird’s cry sounded like “You can’t go on, brother!” — exactly the frustration of a man whose plans are always blocked. The technique is to let scenery speak for feeling: every line is about rivers and hills, and every line is really about his heart.
background: Xin Qiji (1140–1207) grew up in the Jin-occupied north, fought the Jurchens as a young man and fled south to the Song court, where his calls to retake the north were mostly ignored. He wrote this around 1176 while serving as a judicial official in Jiangxi; Zaokou is traditionally linked to the Jin pursuit of a Song empress dowager there in 1129.
pronunciation: 鹧鸪 zhè gū；郁孤台 yù gū tái；中间 zhōng jiān；行人 xíng rén；“愁余”的“余”读 yú，是“我”的意思。
version: 采用通行教材文本。第三句有的版本作“东北是长安”，网站用“西北望长安”。词分上下两阕，各四句。

lines.py: yù gū tái xià qīng jiāng shuǐ
lines.lit: Below Yugu Terrace, the water of the Clear River;
lines.en: Beneath Yugu Terrace the clear river runs —

lines.py: zhōng jiān duō shǎo xíng rén lèi
lines.lit: in it, how many travellers’ tears.
lines.en: how many refugees’ tears are in it?

lines.lit: To the northwest I gaze toward Chang’an;
lines.en: I look northwest toward the old capital;
all I see, alas, are endless hills.
But green hills cannot hold it back:

lines.lit: after all, it flows away east.
lines.en: the river flows east in the end.

lines.lit: Evening on the river just saddens me;
lines.en: Dusk on the water fills me with gloom,

lines.lit: deep in the hills I hear the partridge.
lines.en: and deep in the hills, a partridge calls.

words.en: the Clear River (here the Gan River)
words.note: 指赣江与袁江合流的一段，地名。

words.en: travellers; here people fleeing the war
words.note: 现代汉语指“路上走的人”，这里指逃难的百姓。

words.en: Chang’an, the old capital; here the lost north
words.note: 汉唐的都城，宋词里常用来代指国都。
古义是“可惜”；现代汉语“可怜”多指“值得同情”。
现代汉语也常用，如“遮住”“遮阳”。
“余”是“我”，古汉语常用；“愁”在这里作动词，“使……发愁”。

words.en: Chinese francolin, a kind of partridge
words.note: 鸟名；古人说它的叫声像“行不得也哥哥”。

imagery.name: 江
imagery.zh: 向东奔流、青山挡不住的江水，象征作者收复北方的信念和不可阻挡的大势。
imagery.en: The river that no hill can stop stands for his unshaken hope of winning back the north.

imagery.name: 泪
imagery.zh: 江水里流着“行人泪”，写出金兵南侵时百姓逃难的苦难。
imagery.en: The “travellers’ tears” in the river recall the suffering of people who fled the invasion.

imagery.name: 山
imagery.zh: 挡住望向长安视线的无数座山，比喻收复失地路上的重重阻碍。
imagery.en: The endless hills blocking his view of the capital are the obstacles on the road back north.

imagery.name: 鹧鸪
imagery.zh: 傍晚鹧鸪的叫声像“走不了”，道出壮志难成的苦闷。
imagery.en: The partridge’s cry, heard as “you can’t go on”, voices his frustration at being held back.
